sections.description: This section introduces the case as it initially unfolded in the emergency department, mirroring how a clinician would first encounter the patient. It emphasizes the importance of systematic history-taking and physical examination in generating an initial differential diagnosis when faced with non-specific symptoms such as fever, headache, and mucocutaneous lesions.
subtopics: Presenting symptoms: fever, headache, malaise, persistent hiccups, and arthralgia
Relevant medical history: type 2 diabetes mellitus and implications for clinical assessment
Physical examination findings: vital signs, oral aphthae, folliculitis-like rashes, and euvolemic state
Initial laboratory abnormalities: hyponatraemia, elevated inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR), elevated creatine kinase, and hyperglycaemia
Formulating the initial broad differential diagnosis: infectious, inflammatory, and neoplastic considerations

sections.section_title: Behçet's Disease and Neuro-Behçet's Disease: Clinical Framework
sections.description: This section provides the essential background knowledge on Behçet's disease required to understand the case. It covers the pathophysiology, diagnostic criteria, and clinical manifestations, with particular emphasis on neurological involvement and its atypical presentations.
subtopics: Epidemiology and pathophysiology of Behçet's disease: systemic vasculitis and HLA-B51 association
International Criteria for Behçet's Disease: the point-based scoring system and diagnostic thresholds
Core clinical manifestations: recurrent oral aphthae, genital ulcers, skin lesions, and ocular involvement
Neuro-Behçet's disease: epidemiology, typical onset patterns, and clinical presentations
Aseptic meningitis in neuro-BD: CSF findings and the significance of normal brain MRI in early disease

sections.section_title: SIADH in the Context of Central Nervous System Inflammation
sections.description: This section focuses on the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion as a key complication in this case. It explains the diagnostic criteria, pathophysiological mechanisms linking CNS inflammation to ADH dysregulation, and the clinical consequences of severe hyponatraemia.
subtopics: Diagnostic criteria for SIADH: hypo-osmolar hyponatraemia, elevated urine osmolality, increased urinary sodium, and euvolemia
Pathophysiology: ADH dysregulation and the role of inflammatory cytokines (IL-6) in stimulating ADH release
Etiologies of SIADH: CNS inflammation, malignancy, pulmonary disease, and medication-induced causes
Clinical manifestations of severe hyponatraemia: persistent hiccups and rhabdomyolysis as underrecognized complications
Diagnostic workup to exclude adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism, and other causes of hyponatraemia

sections.description: This section details the systematic process clinicians used to narrow the differential diagnosis. It demonstrates how infectious, neoplastic, and autoimmune conditions were methodically excluded, leading to the diagnosis of concurrent systemic BD and acute neuro-BD complicated by SIADH.
subtopics: Differential diagnosis of fever, headache, and aseptic meningitis: infectious, autoimmune, and neoplastic causes
CSF analysis: interpretation of lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and negative microbiological studies
Exclusion of viral meningoencephalitis (HSV, VZV), bacterial meningitis, and tuberculous meningitis
Evaluation for neurosarcoidosis, CNS lymphoma, and autoimmune encephalitis: role of serum ACE, sIL-2R, and autoantibody testing
Synthesizing the diagnosis: integrating mucocutaneous findings, CSF results, and SIADH to establish acute neuro-BD

sections.section_title: Management Decisions, Treatment Rationale, and Clinical Outcomes
sections.description: This section explains the therapeutic approach taken in this case, including the rationale for colchicine monotherapy, conservative SIADH management, and the avoidance of corticosteroids. It discusses the treatment response and long-term follow-up, highlighting important clinical lessons.
subtopics: Treatment options for BD and neuro-BD: corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, and colchicine
Colchicine mechanism of action: inhibition of neutrophil migration and suppression of IL-1β and IL-6 production
Management of SIADH: fluid restriction, careful sodium monitoring, and avoidance of rapid correction
Clinical response to colchicine monotherapy: resolution of mucocutaneous lesions, neurological symptoms, and hyponatraemia
Long-term follow-up: maintenance therapy, glycaemic control, and absence of recurrence over 4 years
